books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

source: original; stimulus is an original account drawn from the grounding books

stimulus.source_note: Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.10, "The Lunch Counter Sit-ins (1960)"; 5 Steps Ch. 27; Princeton Ch. 12); the Greensboro date, the four students, and the Woolworth's counter are in all three books.
stimulus.text: On February 1, 1960, four Black freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College sat down at the whites-only lunch counter of a Woolworth's store in Greensboro, North Carolina, and asked to be served. They were refused, but they stayed in their seats until the store closed. The next day more students joined them, and within weeks students in other Southern cities were holding sit-ins of their own. The students stayed polite and nonviolent even when crowds shouted at them or poured food on them. Stores that lost business to the sit-ins and to boycotts of their whole business began to serve Black customers.

stem: The sit-ins pressured stores to desegregate mainly through which kind of pressure?

options.text: Military pressure, because federal troops occupied the stores and forced them open
options.misconception: No troops appear in the passage; the stores changed because of lost business.

options.text: Economic pressure, because the protests cost the stores sales and customers
Electoral pressure, because the students voted the store owners out of office
options.misconception: Store owners are not elected, and the passage mentions no voting.

options.text: Diplomatic pressure, because foreign governments protested to Washington about the stores
options.misconception: The passage mentions no foreign government and no diplomacy.

rationales.A: No troops occupied the stores; the passage points to lost business instead.
rationales.B: The passage says stores that lost business to the sit-ins and to boycotts began to serve Black customers.
rationales.C: Store owners hold no office to be voted out of, and the passage mentions no election.
rationales.D: The pressure came from lost sales at home, not from foreign governments.
rationales.general:
1. The students sit at the counter and refuse to leave, blocking normal business.
2. Boycotts add to the loss by keeping other customers away from the whole store.
3. The passage ties the change to that loss: stores that lost business began to serve Black customers.
4. The lever is money, so the pressure is economic.
Remember: A protest that costs a business money gives it a reason to change.
